Make this computer match its nami file

Make your apps and settings match your ~/user.nami; with sudo, system.nami, /etc/nami/system.nami; or the one named

Default: your ~/user.nami (or your config repo's). As root (`sudo nami apply`) or with --system, the system's. Never a file in the current folder by itself. Any other file by its path (`nami apply ./user.nami` in a dotfiles repo); a project's project.nami is for `nami shell` and `nami run`. Keeps the versions in nami.lock; only new packages are resolved.

Or a config repo (github:owner/repo[@branch], or any git URL[@branch]): set this computer up from it in one step. It's cloned into ~/.config/nami (what was there is moved aside) and its nami file applied; the system.nami in this computer's folder (named after it), if any, becomes system.nami (admins). Run it again to pull and apply what changed.

bundle.long_about:
Make your program one file that runs on any Linux

Make your program one file that runs on any Linux distribution (glibc, x86_64), with nothing to install first

From a recipe folder (`nami bundle ./myapp`), a package from the
catalog (`nami bundle jq`), a store path, or a program you built
(`nami bundle ./target/release/myapp`). The file carries the
program's whole closure, glibc
and its loader too; started, it unpacks itself once into ~/.cache
and runs from there, with the computer's own graphics drivers,
fonts, locale and certificates. With --update-url, it updates itself.
`<file> --nami-bundle-help` lists what the file itself can do.

import.long_about:
Turn a Nix setup or old computer into nami files

Turn a Nix setup into nami files (a flake's dev shell into the project's project.nami, home-manager into your ~/user.nami, a NixOS configuration into system.nami), or an old computer into a config repo (`nami import /` on Ubuntu or Debian, or Windows' disk)

Read without Nix (when Nix is installed, `nix eval` fills in what the reader can't). Merges into the target, keeping what's there; what has no nami equivalent is listed, and noted at the end of the file. Applies nothing: run `nami apply` (or `nami shell`) next.

A whole computer (`/`, an old disk mounted somewhere, or Windows' C:) becomes a config repo, ~/nami-config: the apps, Wi-Fi networks (sealed; `sudo` reads them), settings, shell and dotfiles. Your files stay out of it: `--home` says how to move them.

storage.long_about:
See how full the disk is and what nami takes

The disk nami's store is on (on a Mac, the APFS container the Nix Store volume shares), what nami takes, in parts: your apps, apps for everyone, projects' tools, older changes kept for undo, what nothing uses any more and nami's own files. Then the apps that take the most (what removing each would free) and what cleaning up now frees (the nami app's Clean Up: your own old changes, `nami gc --now --user`, then the computer's and what nothing uses, `nami gc --now`). Each store path is counted once, in the first part that uses it; sizes are what the store records for each path (as `nix path-info -S` adds them up), not walked file by file

Keep your setup the same on all your computers

Your setup on all your computers: on, now, status, undo, off

Your user.nami (apps, shell, settings) kept the same on each computer you turn it on on, Ubuntu with nami or namiOS alike, through a private git repo of yours (GitHub's, signed in to in your browser, or any git server's).
